full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J: This Rule is directed against the order dated 9-6-78 of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, refusing an application under Order I, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. A suit for specific performance of an alleged contract was filed by the plaintiff Mosammat Rabeya Begum against defendant No.1 Sree Shankar Karmakar and defendant No.2 since deceased Krishna Rani Karmakar. The Government of Bangladesh was also impleaded as defendant No. 3 in the said suit. It was alleged that the properties originally belonged to one Rama Rani Karmakar who entered into a contract with the plaintiff for sale of the property in question, and executed a bainapatera on 12-7-74 on receipt of an advance of Tk. 15,001. It was agreed that the balance of the consideration will be paid before the execution and registration of the kabala. Rama Rani died on 21-6-76 leaving her heirs defendants 1 and 2 who refused to execute the kabala on 4-8-76. The plaintiff, accordingly, filed the suit for specific performance of the aforesaid contract. Mohammad Shamsul Huq and his wife Mosamaat Hasina Begum claiming to have purchased the property in question from defendant No. 1 alone by a kabala dated 11-9-76 filed an application under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 4-2-78 for being added as defendant to the suit. It was stated in the petition that during the pendency of the suit, they have purchased the properties, and that as the defendants 1 and 2 have no subsisting interest in the properties they are no longer interested in defending the suit property. 'The learned Sub-ordinate Judge rejected the prayer by the impugned order which runs as follows:—

"Parties file haziras. Ptn. Under section 1 rule 10 CPC filed on 4-3-78 is put up. Heard the learned Advocates on both sides. The deft. No. 1 from whom the petitioners alleged to have purchased the disputed property has been himself contesting the suit, and so these petitioners are not necessary parties and the prayer is therefore rejected."

Md Shamsul Huq died thereafter, and the present petitioners before us are his heirs and Mosammat Hassina Begum is his wife and one of the purchasers from defendant No.1

3. Mr Mia Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule contends that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in the exercise of jurisdiction in refusing to add the petitioners as defendants. According to Mr. Gafur, the petitioners have acquired interest in the properties during the pendency of the suit, and, as such, they are interested in the subject-matter of the suit, and their presence is proper, if not, necessary for disposal of the suit. The commences not appear to be soured. There is no dispute at the stage before us that the petitioners are purchasers during the pendency of the suit. That being so, their interest appears to be sufficiently protected by the doctrine of us pendens, Mr Gafur, however, has tried to persuade us to consider the facts and circumstances with reference to certain decision to which we shall presently refer Mr Gafur has referred to a case of Commercial Bank of India (Limited) vs Sabju Saheb, reported in ILR 24 Mad. 252. Reading the judgment, as a whole it appears that the facts are clearly distinguishable and the principle laid down there has no manner of application in the instant case, That was a case of assignment. The next case relied upon by Mr Gafur is that of Laxmi Narayan vs Babu & another reported in AIR 1946 Lahore 33. This case relates to the interpretation of assignment in a pending Suit. An assignment under Order XXII, rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has completely different import and the principle Jairf down there has no application in the facts of the instant case. The case of Prem Sukh Gulgulia vs Habib Ullah reported in AIR 1945 Cal 355 is clearly distinguishable on facts and in law. In this case there was a question as to the applicability of section 66(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and incidentally a question relating to necessary parties in a suit for specific performance of contract arose. We have read the decision between the lines and the facts are so wide and distinguishable that the principle laid down there cannot be applied in the instant case. However, the relevant observations made in the said case are quoted for appreciation of the principle sought to be enunciated there.

"The necessary parties in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale are the parties to the contract, or if they are dead their legal representatives, as also a person who had purchased the property from the vendor after the contract. He is necessary party as lie would be affected, if he is a volunteer, or if a purchaser for value, had purchased with notice of the contract. A person who claims adversely to the Vendor is however, not a necessary party. Where the property stands in the name of person other then the vender, and the suit for specific performance is brought by the purchaser, that person may be joined as a defendant as a proper party on an allegation that he is the benamidar of the vendor but if he appears and contends that he is not the benamidar of the vendor the proper procedure would be to discharge him from the suit, leaving it to the plaintiff in the suit for specific performance to institute a suit against him after he had got the conveyance in execution of the decree for specific performance against his Vendor. This is on the principle that the scope of a suit for specific performance of a contract also ought not to be enlarged and the suit turned also into a title "Suit between one of either of the parties to the contract and a stranger to the contract."

It is premature at this stage to presume whether or not the present petitioners are purchasers for value with notice of the contract,

4. Mr Gafur has next referred to the case of Ram Sworup Singh vs Mahabir Mahaton and another AIR 1960 Pat 135. This is a decision of a single Judge where be has expressed himself in the following terms:—

"Specific performance of contract may be enforced under section 27 against either party to the contract or any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract. In view of this provision in section 27 a prior purchaser ought to impaled a subsequent purchaser as a party to the suit for specific performance, because he is a necessary party inasmuch as, by a decree in favour of the prior purchaser the subsequent purchaser's right in the property is effected since if the sale deed executed by the seller in favour of the prior purchaser is registered, it being of a prior date to the sale in favour of the subsequent purchaser, his title to the land will be immediately affected by it."

The learned Single Judge did not refer to any authority in support of the view taken by him. The facts are also distinguishable.

5. The case of Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan vs Klshorllal Das reported in 7 DLR 157 was referred to by Mr. Gafur. The main question which arose in that case was whether a suit for specific performance of an alleged contract with a prayer for recovery of possession shall be governed by clause (v) or (x) of section 7 of the Court Fees Act. Ibrahim, J held that character of the suit for specific performance of contract is not changed, where the recovery of possession is prayed for and the suit is governed by section 7(x) of the Court Fees Act. Incidentally his Lordship noticed a question whether the subsequent transferees should be impleaded. We may usefully quote the following short extract from the said decision to distinguish the instant case from the facts of the case under reference.

"If the subsequent transferees have taken the property without notice, the consequence, of course, is that the plaintiff's claim cannot succeed; but if they are transferees with notice, as the plaintiff's case is, I do not see why the form should not apply to this case. Specific performance under section 27 of the Specific Relief Act can be claimed against a party to the con-tract as well as any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract."

6. Another decision of Ibrahim, J in the case of Atar Ali vs Abed Ali 5 DLR 470 may be noticed. In this case, the case of Jaharamal Bhatra vs Jatindra Nath Bose 34 CLI 79, was followed. The following extract may be quoted to indicate that the present petitioners are not necessary parties in the facts disclosed.

"It cannot be said that in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale or lease a subsequent transferee is not an interested party; for, a subsequent transferee for value, who has paid his money in good faith without notice of the original contract, is entitled to hold his title against the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of the contract. But the objection in the case is that the lease in favour of the petitioner is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, it having been executed during the pendency of a contentious suit. Where a transfer is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, the transferee is not entitled to hold his title against a party to the suit sought to be affected by the transfer. That appears clearly from these words in section 52 of the Transfer of Properly Act, namely;

“...The property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made there under......”

As his lease is hit by this section, the petitioner has no defence to make against the plaintiff. It is not disputed before me that a suit for specific performance of a contract for lease amounts to a suit in which the right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question."

7. Mr Gafur has drawn our attention to a decision of the West Pakistan High Court in the case of Malik Mohammad Ishaque and another vs Mirza Alamos Ali Beg 21 DLR (WP) 333. This decision has no application in the facts of the instant case. The facts are distinguishable. The next case referred to by Mr. Gafur is the case of Momtaj Ali Karim vs. Abul Hossain 22 DLR 146. In this case also the facts are distinguishable and the principle enunciated there cannot be applied to the facts of the instant case. It has been held that in a case for specific performance of contract, conveyance in favour of subsequent transferee is not affected for want of its registration provided the transferee has paid the purchase money in good faith without notice of the original contract. In such case conveyance is not hit by the doctrine of lis pendens though it is registered after the institution of the suit. The Transferee in such case is protected by the exception of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act.

8. The next case relied upon by Mr. Gafur is that of Fazar Ali vs Abut Kasem Shaikh 22 DLR 240. The facts have no resemblance with the facts of the instant case. The learned Single Judge took the view in the facts of that case alone and the principle cannot be applied in the facts of the instant case. The last case cited by Mr Gufar is the case of Lala Durga Prasad and another vs Lala Deep Chand reported in 1954 SC 934. In this case a subsequent purchaser was impleaded by the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of a contract. The question arose, what should be the form of the decree since the practice of the courts in India was not uniform. It was held that the proper form of the decree was to direct specific performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and direct the subsequent transferee to join the conveyance so as to pass the title, which resides in him to the plaintiff. This principle would have applied if the subsequent transfer was made before the institution of the suit by the plaintiff for specific performance of the contract between plaintiff and his vendor. In such a case the subsequent purchaser will be a necessary party for securing complete title in the event of plaintiff's success in the suit. In the instant case, the subsequent transfer took place during the pendency of the plaintiff's suit for specific performance of the Contract against his vendor. These are all the decisions which Mr. Gafur wished us to consider in support of his contention.

<u>9. We do not intend to extend the scope of a suit for specific performance of an alleged contract and to convert it into a suit for title. In our View section 27 of the Specific Relief Act does not contemplate a suit for adjudication of title between a party to contract and a purchaser pcndentelite from one of the parties to the contract. The case of an assignee stands on a completely different footing. Since the transfer was made by defendant No. I during the pendency of the suit, the petitioners are bound by the results of the suit under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Their title if any, is subject to the result of the suit. In such circumstances their presence is neither necessary nor proper for "effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle, all the questions involved in the suit." Further, if does not stand to reason that a volunteer can throw himself on a plaintiff who alone has the right to claim relief for the cause of action against the persons involved. It may be remembered that the provisions of Order I rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure are necessarily subject to the provisions of Order I rules 1 & 2 and Order 2 rule 3 of the said Code. If the plaintiff fails to implead a necessary party he will suffer the consequences. The plaintiff had no cause of action against the present petitioners who claim to purchasers from defendant No. 1 during the pendency of the suit. In our opinion, the petitioners do not come within the category of persons whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to "enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit." The learned Sub-ordinate Judge appears to have judicially exercised his discretion under the provisions of Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. No error in the exercise of jurisdiction by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge could be pointed out by Mr Gafur.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above, there is no substance in the Rule.</u>

<u>The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

caseno:
First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 2015 
with Civil Rule No. 1164 of 2014
lawyer:
Mr. Md. Reza-E-Morshed Kamal, with Mr. A.K.M Shamsuddin and Mr. Redwan Ullah, Advocates ------ For the Appellant. 
Mr. A. Al-Masud Beg with Mr. M. Miraz Reza, Advocates ------ For the Respondent No.1.
parties:
Harb holding ltd. Represented by its managing director
Vs.
The Premier Bank Limited and others
full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman, J: The instant appeal has been preferred at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant against the order No. 22 dated 25.11.2014 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka in Artha Jari Case No.122 of 2012 allowing the application Under Section 44(1) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and thereby restrained the 3rd party for construction of building or apartment or changing the nature and character of the schedule Property should not be set aside.

2. The appellant-petitioner as 3rd Party appeared before the Court below and filed a written objection against the said application and contested in application for injunction.

3. The material facts, relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are that the opposite party No.1 filed an Artha Rin Suit as plaintiff against the defendant Nos.1-2 being Artha Rin Suit No. 180 of 2011 in the Court of 2nd Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka and obtained an ex-parte judgment and decree on 09.01.2012 and 11.01.2012 respectively for realization of money of Tk. 3,35,48,603.26 as on 17.08.2011. The decree holder hank by dint of the said Judgment and decree filed an Anita Jari Case being No. 122 of 2012 before the concerned Executing Court. The decree-holder Bank filed an application for the purposes of execution of the decree passed by the Hon'ble Court below under Order 21 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 21.06.2012. The plaintiff as a decree holder Bank has obtained a ownership certificate over the schedule property in his favour issued by the Court following due process of law as per Section 33 Sub Section 6(Kha) and 7 under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. The plaintiff decree holder bank after obtaining the Ownership Certificate through Court filed an application for recovery of Khas possession of the schedule land. The Executing Court was pleased to allow the petition and appointed belief for recovery of the land through Court. The appointed belief could not give possession due to obstacle created by Harb Holdings Ltd, the present petitioner and, as such, pray for police force for assisting and executing the same. Thereafter the plaintiff decree holder Bank impleaded the present petitioner as third party in the aforesaid Artha Jari Case No. 122 of 2012 and have filed a petition on 06.11.2014 under Section 44(I) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 for restraining the third Party petitioner from construction of any building or structure in the schedule land until further order.

4. The instant appellant-petitioner as third party appeared before the learned Court below and filed written objection in respect of the said applications on 23.11.2014 and 25.11.2014.

5. The appellant-petitioner has clearly stated the facts in both the written objections in respect of the said applications filed by the Decree holder Bank in accordance with Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. The petition of the Bank Decree holder is false, fabricated and imaginary and has no legal effect and the instant petitioner denied the material allegations of the petition. He has stated that the Bank/Decree holder has not impleaded the present petitioner as defendant in the Artha Rin Suit No. 180 of 2011. The third Party is neither borrower nor in any way related with the loan obtained by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 from the plaintiff Bank/Decree holder and the schedule land of Artha Rin Suit No. 180 of 2011 is quite separate then that of the land of third party instant petitioner and no relation with the third party's construction work. Hence, he has prayed for rejection of the application for injunction. The petitioner has also stated that the Bank/Decree holder with malafide intention to grab the Opposite party's land most illegally impleaded him as 3id Party in the said Artha Jari Case No. 122 of 2012 and trying to take forceful possession in the 3rd party's owned undisputed land which is free from all encumbrances and the application is not maintainable in the eye of law and liable to be rejected.

6. In the said written objection the petitioner as 3rd party has also stated their case and the land in suit is as the land of C.S Dag No. 171 originally belonged to Shahara Khatun and she died leaving behind Shamsuddin Bepari, Wahed Beapri and daughter Dud Meher as only legal heirs who owned and possessed the land and their names have been correctly recorded in the C.S Record in equal share of 8 annas each the area of land is 220 ajutangsha. After the death of Shamsuddin R.S Record was prepared and published in the names of Badruddin, Sirajuddin, Nazimuddin and Nasiruddin as legal heirs of late Shamsuddin and Bilkish Begum wife of late Advocate Meozuddin. 1800 Ajutangsha of land has been recorded in the name of Bilkish Begum in R.S Dag 3528 and 3870 ajutangsha has been recorded in the name of Badruddin. Nazimuddin, Shirajuddin and Nasiruddin in R.S Dag No. 3528. The description of land has been described in the plaint of Artha Rin Suit No. 180 of 2011 and Artha Jari Case No. 122 of 2012 is quite different and dissimilar with the land of the Opposite party No.3. The plaintiff decree holder Bank with ulterior motive and to grab the property of 3rd party described an imaginary description of land in the schedule of Artha Jari Case which is liable to be rejected. The Bank authority has no legal right to stop the construction of the 3rd party who purchased land which is no way connected with the land property of the Bank "Harbour Kallani Scheme" and decreed property of the Bank.

7. The learned Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, after hearing both the parties by its order dated 25.11.2014 in Artha Rin Case No. 122 of 2012 allowed the application for injunction.

8. Being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 25.11.2014, the 3rd party as appellant preferred the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal pending hearing of FMA filed an application for stay.

9. At the time of issuance of the Civil Rule No.1164 (FM) 2014 the Court stayed the operation of the impugned judgment and Order which was passed on 25.11.2014 in Artho Jari Case No. 122 of 2012 up to 09.01.2017.

10. Thereafter, this matter was fixed and posted in the list for hearing.

11. Mr. Md. Reza-E-Murshed Kamal with Md. A.K. Shamsuddin and Redwan Ullah, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the appellant has submitted that the Court below erred in law in passing the impugned judgment and Order upon misconception and misconstrued the provision of law under Sections 44 and 57 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and, as such, erred in law in the facts and circumstances as well as law for which the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

12. He has further submitted that having the decree holder Bank as petitioner in the Court below admitted that the 3rd party was not Party in the proceeding of the Artho Rin case and filed the application against the 3rd party in the Artho kid Case which is beyond the scope of Artho Rin Ain. So, the Court has no legal authority to restrain the 3rd party in accordance with law as the 3rd party neither borrower nor guarantor in the loan in question and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

13. He has added that the learned Judge of Artho Rin Adalat in disposing the application has failed to understand the consequence of the decree as the decree has not passed against the 3rd party. The petitioner categorically described that the schedule land of the decree Jail Case No. 122 of 2012 and schedule land has been described in the written objection by the company is not identical, rather, quite distinguishable as admitted by the decree holder Bank petitioner as well as the learned Judge in spite of such fact restrained the 3rd party petitioner herein by an order of injunction which cannot rather, which collies within the purview of misuse of judicial jurisdiction which must be stayed and set aside by this Hon'ble Court, otherwise judicial misconception and the mismanagement in the judiciary will continue.

14. On the other hand, Mr. A. Al Masud Begh and Mr. M. Miraz Raza appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1.

15. Mr. Miraz Raza, the learned Advocate has submitted that the 3rd party started construction in the suit Property of the execution case which belongs to the Bank decree holder respondent.

16. In that view of the matter they invoked jurisdiction of Sections 44/57 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 seeking redress against the 3rd party. Ile has further submitted that though the Court below clearly opined that the property of the 3rd Party is quite distinguishable from the suit land of the execution case, however, the Judge of the Artho Rin Adalat restrained the 3rd party not to construct building in the property of the decree holder which has been described in the schedule of the execution case as well as the application under Section 44/57 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Therefore in passing the impugned Order, the Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat neither acted without jurisdiction nor passed the same in flagrant violation of any legal proposition of the law. Hence, the impugned judgment and order does not call for interference by this Court.

17. We have considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates of the respective parties. We have gone through the impugned Order dated 25.11.2014 passed by the Judge, Artho Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka in Artha Jari Case No. 122 of 2012 and perused the record.

<u>18. On perusal of the impugned order dated 25.11.2014, it appears that the learned Judge passed the impugned Order mentioning the case schedule of Artho Rin Jari Case No. 122 of 2012, however, it reflects in the ordering portion that the Court has granted injunction mentioning the name of the 3rd party Harb Holdings Limited in the schedule land of the Artho Jari Case No. 122 of 2012. Further perusal of the impugned Order it appears that the learned Judge of Artho Rin Adalat noticed in the judgment that the suit property has been described in the schedule of the execution case and the land claimed and construction work has been doing by the 3rd Party are quite disguisable and separate holding which not the mortgage party. However, we are of the view that since Courts itself found that properties of the 3rd party are not the property of the mortgage land of the schedule of the execution case, so, passing the impugned order cannot be sustained in law. Therefore, we cannot but to opine that entertaining the application by the Court against the 3rd party does not come within the purview of sections 44/57 of the Artho Rin Ain, 2003.</u>

<u>19. According to provision of sections 44/57 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 can not be applicable against the 3rd party as the fact and circumstances do not support that they are constructing building in the schedule land of the execution case. Therefore, as per provision of the quoted sections cannot be invoked against the 3rd party who is neither loanee nor mortgagor. Rather, it is crystal clear from the opinion of the Court below the property belongs to the 3rd party who has right, title and interest. There is specific provision of law under Order 21 of the Civil Procedure for execution a decree. The decree holder Bank without taking proper course of law before the Court below take the illegal action against the 3rd party which neither in accordance with law nor take any steps in the Artho jari Case to protect the right and title of the decreed property as obtained against the judgment debtor in Artho Rin case.</u>

20. The executing Court has no jurisdiction to act beyond the decree and cannot act as per provision of sections 44 and 57 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain to pass an order of injunction in a non suit land which does not belong to borrower or mortgagor.

21. As such we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, 3rd Party. The submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the Opposite Party does not bear any merit.

22. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost of Tk.50,000/- which to be paid by

the decree holder Bank to the appellant 3rd party within 60 days from the date of receipt

of the Judgment. Failing of which the appellant 3rd party can take shelter of law to recover money from the decree holder Bank in accordance with law.

23. The Office is directed to communicate the judgment to the Court below as well as

opposite party decree holder premier Bank Limited.

24. The Civil Rule No.1164 (F.M) 2014 is disposed of with the above observation.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman. J.- This appeal by the defendant-appellant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is directed against Order No. 9 date 22.5.86 passed by Mr. M.I. Hafiz, Subordinate Judge-in-Charge of Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Money Execution Case No. 3 of 1986.

2. Facts of the case are as follows-Plaintiff decree-holder respondent Rafique Ahmed, Proprietor M/S. Karnafully Shipping and Trading Corporation,91 Agrabad Commercial Area, Chittagong instituted Money Suit No. 244 of 1980 in the then 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong (since abolished and merged with the Second Court of Subordinate Judge,Chittagong) against 10 defendants including Judgment-debtor defendant No.1 M/s Saturn Commercial Enterprises(having head office in Dhaka and Branch office in Chittagong. 

3. The suit was contested by defendant no. 2 Messrs Ednasa Shipping Company Limited, Hong Kong, defendant No 1 Captain Wong. Jinu Kong, the master of the vessel M. V. Lennia (Defendant no.1 Messrs Saturn Commercial Enterprises and defendant no. 2 Messrs Ednasa Shipping Company Limited represented by defendant No. 3) and defendant No. 6 Messrs. Hegge and Company (Bangladesh) Ltd., Spencer's Building, Agrabad Commercial Area, Chittagong. The learned Subordinate Judge in the said Money Suit decreed the suit for recovery of TK. 9,00,000/-on contest against the defendants 2, 3 and 6 and exported against defendant 1, 4 and 5 with costs. The plaintiff was allowed to get an amount of Tk. 9,00,000/- from defendants 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 with pendent lite interest of Tk.15% per annum from the date of filing of the suit till realization of the decree tall dues. The defendants 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 ere directed to pay the decree tall amount to the plaintiff within 90 days from the date of judgment and order dated 4.1.84. A Division Bench of the High Court to which I was a party in F.A. No. 6 of 1984 (preferred by appellants defendant no. 2 M/s. Ednasa, Hong Kong, Defendant no. 3 Captain Wong Jium Kong and defendant No. 6 Messrs Hegge & Company (Bangladesh) Ltd. Agrabad, Chittagong) allowed the appeal in part, set aside the decree passed against defendant Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 without cost but decreed the suit ex parte against defendant no. 1 Messrs Saturn Commercial Enterprises, Singapore for Tk. 5,75,829.02 with proportionate cost and interest pendent lite at the rate of Tk. 10% per annum from the date of institution of the suit till recovery of the same. No appeal was preferred against the said judgment and decree passed by this Court. Plaintiff-decree-holder Rafique Ahmed, Proprietor, Karnafully Shipping and Trading Corporation (Respondent no. 1. in this appeal) put the decree into execution on 19.3.86 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong being Money Execution Case No. 3 of 1986 in accordance with the provisions of Rule 11(2) of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

4. On 19,3,86 plaintiff decree holder stated, inter alia, in an application under Order 21, Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code that he obtained a decree ex parte against the defendant no. 1 Saturn Commercial Enterprises, Singapore for Tk. 5,75,829.03with proportionate costs and pendent lite interest at the rate of Tk.10% per annum, that defendant No. 6 by letter Ext. 2(f) dated 3.10.80 informed the plaintiff that defendant no 2 M/S. Ednasa Shipping Co. Ltd., Hong Kong was holding U.S. dollars 14,326.00 on defendant no. 1's account and that defendant No.5 Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (the present appellant) was holding U.S. dollars 34,296.60 payable to judgment-debtor defendant no. 1 Messrs Saturn Commercial Enterprises, Singapore, that unless the aforesaid amount belonging to defendant no. 1 judgment-debtor lying in the possession and in the hands of the aforesaid Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is attached and unless the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is prohibited by an order from giving it over to the judgment-debtor defendant no. 1, the plaintiff decree-holder will be greatly prejudiced and will suffer irreparable loss and injury. On 19.3.86 this application was placed before the Executing Court which fixed 20.3.86 for hearing the petition and for passing the order in presence of the Advocates. On 20.3.86 the Executing court issued writ of prohibitory order of attachment upon the Bangladesh-Shipping Corporation under Order 21, Rule 46(1)(a)(c) C.P.C. fixing 20.4.86 for hearing. On 8.4.86 the decree-holder filed an application praying for a direction to the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation having branch office in Chittagong to deposit an amount of Tk. 8,75;739/97 in the Executing Court. The executing Court allowed the prayer and directed the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to deposit the said amount in the Court. In the present case the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is a garnishee, that is)a third party who is asked not to pay money -to the judgment-debtor because the latter is to satisfy the decree obtained by the decree-holder. 

5. On 20.4.86 the appellant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation filed an application stating that the learned Subordinate Judge,Second Court in Money Execution case No. 3 of 1986 by his order dated 20.3.86 directed Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to restrain itself from making any payment of Tk. 8,75,799/79 to the judgment-debtor Saturn Commercial Enterprises, Singapore, that on 10.4.86 the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation was informed by another order of the Court to deposit the attached amount to Court, but instead of mentioning the correct amount of Tk. 8,75,739.97 by mistake the Court mentioned Taka 8,93,451/47 which mistake should be corrected, that the plaintiff decree-holder filed a suit regarding the same money in the Second Court of Munsif, Chittagong being other Suit No.116 of 1985 wherein the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation was made defendant no. 1 and the said suit has not yet been disposed of, that it is necessary that the said Other suit no.116 of 1985 should be disposed of before the petitioner(Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) is compelled to make any deposit (the said suit no.116 of 1985 was subsequently withdrawn by the plaintiff decree-holder on 27.4.86) that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation had not yet got any instruction from the judgment-debtor regarding the said order of attachment and that in these circumstances the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation had to pray before the Court for one month's time to make the deposit of such amount as would be ordered by the Executing Court. The learned Subordinate Judge there upon' passed the following order No. 5 dated 20.4.86:- 

"The Bangladesh Shipping Corporation files a petition along with a fresh power praying for time for depositing the decretal amount into the Court on the ground stated in the petition. Copy served Considered. The prayer is allowed.To.10.5.86 for depositing the decretal amount in Court by the applicant as 'prayed for:" 

6. On 10.5.86 appeIlant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation filed another application before the executing Court stating that immediately on receipt of notice of the said Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation sent an urgent telex to the judgment-debtor for information but unfortunately no instruction as yet had been received, that it was necessary that the petitioner received instruction from the judgment-debtor for the disposal of the money in question as otherwise the petitioner might be sued by the judgment-debtor in a foreign Court which would also make the vessels of the petitioner liable for attachment causing huge loss and that it was necessary that the petitioner should be given 15 days time for receiving necessary instruction from the judgment- debtor. 

7. On a consideration of this application the Executing Court passed the following order No.6 dated 10,5,86:- 

"Decree-holder files hazira. The applicant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation by petition prays for time to deposit the decrial amount in Court on the grounds stated in the petition. Copy served. No objection(raised by decree- holder if time is allowed) for only 7 days Considered. The prayer is allowed. To 17.5,86 for depositing decrial amount in Court as prayed for by the applicant." 

8. On 17.5.86 the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation filed an application before the executing Court stating that the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation sought instruction from the Messrs Saturn Commercial Enterprise for making payment that they informed petitioner that there was a: dispute regarding the money between some of the defendants, that the petitioner had been instructed to pray for time for further instruction and that the petitioner should be allowed time for further 7 days. The executing Court by its order No. 7. dated 17.5 .86 noted that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has prayed for further time for depositing the decretal amount of Tk. 8,75,739/97 on the ground stated in the petition that subsequently Bangladesh Shipping Corporation filed another petition along with fresh vakalatnama praying for one month's time to deposit the decretal amount in Court on the ground stated in the petition, that the decree-holder also filed a petition praying for directing the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to deposit the said attached amount in Court on the ground stated in the petition and ordered that 18.5.86 was fixed for hearing the matter. On 18.5.86 the executing Court heard both sides and rejected the Bangladesh Shipping corporation’s petition dated 17.5.86 and allowed lucre-holder's petitions dated 17.5.86 and 18.5.86 and directed the decree-holder to take step, if any, by 2.5.86. On 22.5.85 a prayer was made on behalf the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation before the executing Court stating as follows:- 

" The original Money Suit No. 244 of 1980 and F.A. No. 6 of 1984 has been decreed against M/S. Saturn Commercial Enterprise (judgment-debtor) for a sum of Tk. 8,93,451/47 (actually Tk. 8,75,839/97) with interest. On the prayer of the decree-holder the Honorable Court was pleased to order this petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) not to give the amount to M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise (judgment-debtor) or others. The fact remains that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is not in any way connected with M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise and does not hold any account in the name of M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise and thereby the question of remittance of money to M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation does not arise at all .In the instant case Bangladesh Shipping Corporation acted as agent of the Ministry of Food, Govt.of Bangladesh who acted as Charterer for M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise. Thereby in the instant case Bangladesh Shipping Corporation holds all the accounts of Ministry of Food and transactions with the Ministry of Food, Govt. of Bangladesh only and is not in any way connected with M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise (judgment-debtor). The petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has got no money (debt) payable to M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise (the Judgment-debtor) and therefore, the instant Money Execution case (M.Ex. 3/86) automatically fails in its result. It is, therefore, prayed that the Court would be pleased to dismiss the Money Executing Case (M.Ex. 3/86) against the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation with compensatory cost to the petitioner". 

The Executing Court thereupon passed the following impugned order No. 9 dated 22.5.86:- 

"Bangladesh Shipping Corporation by a petition supported by an affidavit prays for dismissing this Execution case against the petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) on the ground embodied therein. Copy served with objection. Decree-holder also files a petition praying for passing an order to proceed with the execution case against Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, Toynbee Circular Road, Motijheel C.A., Dhaka, having branch office in Chittagong on the ground embodied therein. Copy served with serious objection. Heard Advocates. The prayer of the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is rejected and the prayer of the decree-holder is allowed. The decree holder may take steps if any by 24.5.86." 

Being aggrieved by the said order the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has preferred this appeal. 

9. On 28.5.85 Civil Rule 192(F.M.) of 1986 was obtained by Bangladesh Shipping Corporation from this Court and all further proceedings of the aforesaid Money Execution case was stayed till the disposal of the present Appeal. 

10. In Civil Rule No.192(F.M.) of 1986 it was stated in the counter-affidavit on behalf of the decree-holder opposite party no. 1 that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has already admitted in the executing Court that they have got money on account of defendant no. 1. the judgment- debtor, that in the Money Execution Case No. 3 of 1986 against the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation the executing Court issued on 20.3.86 prohibitory order of attachment upon the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation under Order 21, Rule 46(1)(a)(c) C.P.C., that the executing Court on 8.4.86 directed the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to deposit the decrial amount of Tk. 8,75,739/97 including interest and cost, that the executing Court allowed the prayer of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and granted time till.10.5.86 to deposit the said decrial amount in the Court on the ground stated in the petition of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and that then extended time till 17.5.86 on the prayer of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, that the executing Court rejected further prayer of Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and directed the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to deposit attached amount in Court and also directed the decree-holder to take steps and by order dated 25.5.86 the listed moveable properties, such as motor vehicles of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation were attached and given in the Jimma of Mr. Mozaharul Islam, Deputy General Manager(Administrator) on 26.5.86, that the petitioner Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has already admitted the position that the aforesaid amount on account of the judgment-debtor M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise is lying with them, that they were praying for time only for seeking instruction from the judgment-debtor in respect of this matter, i.e. satisfaction of the decree passed against the judgment-debtor, that subsequently by ill advice in order to harass the decree-holder and by changing lawyer by fresh power with malafide motive and for illegal gain, the petition was filed with false statements, that the petitioner is estopped under the law from making contrary or contradictory statements to what they have stated in the three earlier petitions in writing and by changing lawyer the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation stated falsely that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is not in any way connected with the M/S. Saturn Commercial Enterprise and does not hold any moiled on account of M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise and therefore the question of remittance of money to M/s. On this ground Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahrnan the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff decree-holder opposite party, submits that the present appeal should be dismissed on merit He also submits that since an order under Order 21 Rule 46(21)(a)(c) of the C.P.C.is not appealable under order 43 Rule 1 C.P.c. the appeal is not maintainable and that on this ground also the appeal should fail. 

11. Mr. Ahsanul Kabir, the learned Advocate for the appellant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation shows S.C. Sarkar's Book on the Code of Civil Procedure; 3rd edition(l945) page 552-553 and 5th edition 1983 page 598 and submits that by notification No.1854-G dated 26.1.1935, Rules 46A, 46B, k46C, 46D, 46E, 46F, 46G, 46H were added after Rule 46 of Order 21 C.P.C. by the Calcutta High Court and that consequently the said rules 46A-46H of Order 21 were treated to be the existing law of the then East Bengal (later East Pakistan) within the jurisdiction of the then High Court of Dacca under the relevant laws made on the eve of independence on the 14th August, 1947 and those Rules 46A to 46H of Order 21. C.P.c. continue to be the existing laws in Bangladesh as defined in Article 152(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. In the 3rd Edition (1954) at page 553 of S.C. Sarker's book of the Code Of Civil Procedure it is rightly noted that the High Court of East Bengal and Assam have the same amendments as added Rules 46A-H of the Calcutta High Court (by notification no.1854-G dated 26.1.1935. The learned Advocate for the appellant points out that Order 21 Rule, 46H provides that an order made under Rules 46B 46C, or 46E of Order 21 shall be appealable as a decree. He also submits that rule 46C of Order 21 C.P.C. provides that where the garnishee disputes liability, the Court may order that any issue or question necessary for the determination of liability shall be tried as if it were an issue in a suitand upon the determination of such issue the Court shall make such order or orders upon the parties as may seem just.He also refers to Rules 58-63 of order 21 C.P.C. regarding investigation of claims to, and objections to attachrnent of, attached property in execution of a decree. 

12. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the earned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent decree-holder refers to the decision in the as of Md. Nurul Islam Vs Abdur Rasnid & others exported in 1983 BW (AD) 310 and submits that nonce the said Calcutta High Court Rules 46A-46H  Order 21 C.P.C. has not been incorporated in the ode of Civil Procedure as published by the v1inistry of law and Parliamentary Affairs of the Government of Bangladesh in 1979 Edition or even in the latest Edition published in 1984 (corrected upto 31st June,1984). those amendments made by the Calcutta High Court cannot be treated as laws in Bangladesh. In the case of Md. Nurul Islam Vs. Md. Abdur Rashid and others 1983 BW(AD) 310 the Appellate Division seems to have taken the view that rule 2-A of Order XVIII of the Code of. Civil Procedure (which was added by the Calcutta high Court by Notification No.15165-GdateQ 8.11.l927) is a "provision in India", it is not so in Bangladesh. That Rule 2-A of Order XVIII of the Civil Procedure Code of Calcutta High Court though added in 1927 is not the law of this Country, Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman submits, will be gathered from the following observation of he Appellate Division in the case of Md. Nurul Islam Vs. Md. Abdur Rashid and others, 1983 3LD (A.D) 310:-  

Although we are not in favour of encouraging a procedure which is not covered by any express provision of the Code, we shall, however, refrain from interfering with the two orders in view of the special facts and circumstances of the present case.

It is noted that there is a provision namely, Dryer XVIII Rule 2-A of the C.P.C. in India (there hoeing no High Court called High Court of Indian or Indian High Court,it obviously refers to Rule 2A of Order 18 added in 1927 by the Calcutta High Court) which runs as follows :-

 "2A. Notwithstanding anything contained in clauses (1) and (2) of rule 2, the court may for sufficient reasons go on with the hearing, although the evidence of the party having the right to begin has not been concluded, and may also allow either party to produce any witness at any stage of the suit." 

The High Court Division in the fact and circumstances of the case there being no provision to meet the situation arising in the present case had, therefore, fallen upon section 151 C.P.C. to meet the ends of justice." 

It will appear from the above quoted decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Md. Nurul Islam Vs. Md. Abdur Rashid and others reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 310 that the question whether the Rules added by the Calcutta High Court before the independence of the country on the 14th August,1947 which continued to be "the existing law" in East Bengal(later East Pakistan) within the Jurisdiction of the High Court of judicature at Dacca still continue to be the existing law of Bangladesh under the Constitution of Bangladesh which came into force on 16th December, 1972 after the liberation of the country has not been at all raised, argued, discussed and decided in the aforesaid decision.Be that asit may, it will appear from the Code of Civil Procedure as amended by Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1983 that in Order XLIII, in Rule (1) of the C.P.C., after clause (i) the following new clauses were inserted, namely:- 

" (ii) an order under rule 60 of Order XXI releasing property from attachment, 
(iii) an Order under rule 61 of Order XXI disallowing a claim to property attached." 

The impugned order against which the appellant has come is an order under rule 61 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure disallowing. a claim made by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (garnishee) to the to the property attached by the executing Court and as such it may be treated as appealable under rule (l)(II) of Order XLIII C.P.C. as amended by Ordinance XLVIII of 1983., Before the, said amendment made in 1983 even if appeal did not lie, revision under section 115(1) C.P.C. would lie before this Court. 

13. Rule 46C of Order XXI provides that where the garnishee disputes liability, the Court may order that any issue or question necessary for the determination of liability shall be tried as if it were an issue in a suit and upon the determination of such issue shall make such orders upon the parties as may seem just.Even if Rule 46C as aforesaid is not treated to be the Rule adopted in Bangladesh, the fact in this case remains that on 19.3.86 plaintiff decree-holder filed an application under order XXI rule 46 stating that for satisfaction of his decree the amount of U.S. dollars 34,296.60 held by defendant No. 5 Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (present appellant) on account of judgment-debtor defendant no.1 M/S, Saturn Commercial Enterprise, Singapore. should be attached forthwith and that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (appellant) should be prohibited by an order from giving' the money over to the judgment- debtor Messrs Saturn Commercial Enterprise, Singapore (defendant no. 1 in the suit) and the executing Court by its order No. 2 dated 20.3.86 and order No. 3 dated 3.4.86 allowed this prayer, that then on 20.4.86 the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation prayed for one month's time to make the deposit of such amount as may be ordered by the executing court after receipt of instruction from the judgment-debtor regarding the order of attachment and that finally on 22.5.86 the garnishee Bangladesh Shipping Corporation came up with an application stating "that it has been stated by the Decree-holder that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation holds an account Saturn Enterprise with it for a sum of Tk. 8,93,451/47, the decreed amount with interest, that on the prayer of the Decree- Holder the executing Court was pleased to order this petitioner(Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) not to give the amount to M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise or others that the fact remains that, on this petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) is not in any way connected with the M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise and does not hold and owe any account in the name of M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise and thereby the question of remittance of money to M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation does not arise at all, that in the instant case Bangladesh Shipping Corporation acted as agent of tire Ministry of Food, Govt. Bangladesh who acted as Charterer for M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise, that thereby in this instant case this petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) holds all the accounts of Ministry of Food and transactions with the Ministry of Food, Govt.of Bangladesh only and not in any way connected with M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise, that this petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) has got no money payable debt) to M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise the judgment-debtor and thereby the instant Money Execution case (M.Ex. 3/86) automatically fails". The appellant (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) who on these grounds prayed for dismissal of the Money Execution Case No. 3/86, in fact prayed for releasing the property attached by the executing Court by order No. 2 dated 20.3.86 and order No. 3 dated 3.4.86 and denied the claim of the judgment-debtor that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation holds any money of account of the judgment-debtor M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise, Singapore. It appears that after this application was filed by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation on 22.5.86 the executing Court without investigation of the claim preferred to and objection made to attachment of the money in question simply ordered by its Order no. 9 dated 22.5.86 as follows:- 

"The prayer of the petitioner (Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) is rejected." 

and directed the decree holder to take steps, if any by 24.5.86. 

The executing Court has given no reason whythe Court rejected the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation's petition filed on 22.5.86 wherein it was stated that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation does not-hold any money on account of the judgment debtor M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise and that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation holds all the accounts of transactions with the Ministry of Food who acted as Charterer for M/s.Saturn Commercial Enterprise. 

14. The executing: Court in these circumstances has to follow the provisions of  of Rules 58,59,60 and 61 of Order 21 C.P.C., make investigation of the claim preferred to, or any objection made to the attachment of the money inquestion, ask the parties to adduce evidence and upon such investigation either disallow the claim of the garnishee that the money in question was, at the time it was attached, not in its possession on account of or in trust for the judgment debtor or release the property (money) from attachment wholly or to such extent as it thinks fit on being satisfied that the garnishee was not possessing the property(money) on account of or in trust for the judgment debtor. In the case of Sardhri Lal Vs. Ambika Pershad, 15 Indian Appeals, 1123 I.L.R. 15 Cal 521 (P.C) the Privy Council observed, "The Code does not prescribe the extent to which the investigation should go; and though in some cases it may be very proper that there should be as full an investigation as if a suit were instituted for the very purpose of trying the question, in other cases it may also be the most prudent and proper course to deliver an opinion on such facts as are before the court at the time, leaving the aggrieved party to bring the suit which the law allows to him(See rule 63 of Order 21)". Rules 59 to 62 of Order 21 C.P.C. in fact provide for a summary investigation into possession as distinct from a. thorough trial of ultimate right. 

15. It was thus the duty of the Executing Court in this case to ask the decree-holder to establish by adducing evidence that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation was holding the money on account of or in trust of the judgment-debtor M/s. Saturn Commercial Enterprise, Singapore and also to ask the garnishee to substantiate its objection and after hearing both sides in this respect and after examining the evidence including the necessary documents and connected papers to be filed by both the parties the executing Court was to write out a clear order giving reason why it was disallowing the prayer made by the alleged garnishcc-
Bangladesh Shipping Corporation in which case the court would have to release the property which stood attached. Accordingly we arc of the view that (he executing Court should re-hear the application made by the appellant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation on- 22.5.86 giving opportunity to the decree-holder to controvert the assertion made by the appellant Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and also to give the decree-holder as well as the alleged garnishee Bangladesh Shipping Corporation an opportunity to establish their claim by adducing evidence including relevant documents and connected papers and decide the question in issue after hearing both the parties.It is also obvious that the question whether the garnishee Bangladesh Shipping Corporation has admitted the plaintiff decree- holder's assertion that the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation was holding u.s. dollar 14,326.00 on account of the judgment debtor has also to be examined and decided by the executing court after giving both parties opportunity to adduce evidence and after hearing the contentions made by the parties. 

16. In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost.The impugned order No. 9 dated 22.5.86 rejecting the petition dated 22.5.86 filed by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation is set aside and the executing Court is directed to dispose of the aforesaid application of the. Bangladesh Shipping Corporation filed on 22.5.86 in the light of the observations made above as expeditiously as possible preferably within two month from the date of receipt of this order.

full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: This Rule was issued at the instance of decree-holder petitioner Tripura Modern Bank Ltd., in liquidation against order dated 22.8.85 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Money Execution Case No. 67 1968 striking out the said execution case.

2. It appears that the said Money Execution Case No. 67 of 1968 was filed by the decree holder for realisation of the sum Tk. 1,11,915/13 with interest on the decreetal dues of Tk. 1,03,532.75 in pursuance of on order passed and certificate granted on 30.4.64 by the then High Court of Dhaka in Matter No. 31 of 1962 under section 63 of the Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962 after the first execution case being Money Execution Case No. 55 of 1966 was dismissed for default on 12.7.67. It further appears that the judgment-debtor filed several cases under the now repealed section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and he failed in all the cases except in Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1971 which was allowed by judgment and order dated 16.1.75. The petitioner preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1975 against the said order in this Court and by judgment dated 18.1.81 the said appeal was allowed and the judgment and order of the executing court was set aside and directed to dispose of the execution proceeding in accordance with law. It further appears that no appeal was preferred by the judgment-debtor against the aforesaid judgment of this Court. It further appears that on the application of the decree holder the executing Court on 8-3-83 passed order that the execution case shall proceed and by order dated 20.11.83 brought on record the names of the opposite parties as heirs of the judgment-debtor who was alleged to have died in the meantime. The opposite parties thereafter filed an objection petition challenging the said order and the court below after hearing the parties by the impugned order dated 22.8.85 held that the decree passed in the said First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1975 was a nullity and as such execution case was liable to be struck out and rejected. The Court below relied on the decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Bishnu Bijoy Vs. Chandra Buoy reported in AIR 1955 Cal. 281 and of the Bombay High Court in the case of Trimbak Vs. Copal reported in AIR 1947 Bombay 480 to come to the conclusion that the appeal against the order in the execution proceeding having abated the decree of the appellate Court was a nullity.

3. Mr. Abdul Mannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that the Court below was wholly wrong to hold that the appeal filed by the petitioner in the High Court Division abated for not substituting the names of the heirs of the sole judgment-debtor respondent in whose favour the executing court passed the order in the proceeding under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure striking out the execution case in as much as the said appeal was the continuation of the execution proceeding and that it was the High Court Division which decided the appeal and not the executing Court to find whether the said appeal abated or not and the executing court could at best refer the matter to the High Court Division to decide the question. In support of his contention the learned Advocate relied on the decision in the case of Hakeem Syed Mohammad Taqui Vs. Patch Bahadur Singh reported in AIR 1929 Pat. 565 (FB) and the case of Ram Saran Vs. Prithevi Nath Singh reported in AIR 1952 Patna 267. He further submitted that in the absence of section 47 of the Code the executing court exceeded its jurisdiction in passing the impugned order.

4. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submitted that appeal against an order in an execution proceeding will abate with the death of the judgment-debtor respondent and relied on the two decisions referred to by the Court below in the impugned order and as such the executing Court did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned order.

5. While deciding the case reported in AIR 1947 Bombay 480 Gajendra Kar, J as his Lordship then was noticed all the decisions of the several High Courts in the Indian Sub-continent and found that except the Patna High Court in AIR 1929 Pat. 565 (FE), all the High Courts have taken the view that appeals from orders in execution proceedings do not fall within the provisions of Order 22 rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that to such appeals the rules as to abatement contained in rules 3 and 4 of the said Order shall apply. Patna High Court in the aforesaid Full Bench decision held that rule 12 of Order 22 applies not only to proceedings in execution of a decree or order in the Court of first instance but also to appeals against orders passed in course of such proceedings and as such the appeal before that Court arising from an order passed in an execution case did not abate on the death of the respondent though the appellant failed to apply to make the legal representative of the deceased respondent a party to the appeal within the time prescribed by law. Calcutta High Court in the aforesaid decision reported in AIR 1955 Cal. 281 noticed that Full Bench decision of the Patna High Court was passed relying on the decision of the Lahore High Court reported in AIR 1923 Lahore 560 and the said decision was overruled in the case of Arjuda Prosad Vs. Sham Sundar reported in AIR 1947 Lahore 13 (FB) and reiterated the view held by Gajindra Kumar, J in AIR 1947 Born 480 and dissenting view of Das, J in AIR 1929 Pat. 565 (FB) without referring to the same. In all the aforesaid decisions except AIR 1929 Pat. 565 (FB) the learned Judges were of the view that since no distinction has been made between an appeal arising from a suit and an appeal arising from execution proceeding of a decree the provision applicable to appeals will guide all the appeals irrespective of their origin and as such under the provision of rule 11 of Order 22 provisions of rules 3 and 4 of the said Order will apply to appeals and hence on the failure of the appellant to bring on record the names of legal representatives of the deceased respondent within the period of time allowed by law the appeal arising from an execution proceeding will also abate. Whereas the majority view of the learned Judges in the aforesaid Full Bench decision of the Patna High Court is that the appeal arising from an execution proceeding is nothing but continuation of the execution proceeding and when there is no abatement of execution proceeding on the failure of the decree holder to bring on record that legal representatives of the deceased judgment-debtor as provided under rule 12 of Order 22 of the Code the appeal arising from such an execution proceeding cannot also abate.

6. Rules 11 and 12 of Order 22 of the Code read as follows:—

"11. In the application of this Order to appeals, so far as may be, the word "plaintiff" shall be held to include an appellant, the word "defendant" a respondent, and the word "suit" an appeal.

<u>12. Noting in rules 3, 4 and 8 shall apply to proceeding in execution of a decree or order".</u>

<u>From the aforesaid rule 11 it appears that provisions of the Order applicable in suits shall be applicable in appeals and the plaintiff shall be held to include an appellant and defendant shall be held to include a respondent. As such rules 3 and 4 of the Order applicable to plaintiff and defendant in the suit shall apply to the appellant and respondent in the appeal. So it is clear that there will be abatement of the appeal arising from a suit under the provisions of rules 3 and 4 of the Order. Since rule 11 does not refer to execution case or decree holder and judgment-debtor we agree with the view that rules 3 and 4 of the Order will not apply to an appeal from an order in an execution proceeding and there will be no abatement of the appeal from an order in an execution case. Moreover an appeal from an order in an execution case is nothing but the continuation of the execution case and since rules 3 and 4 the Order do not apply to execution case as provided under the provisions of rule 12 of the Order such appeal cannot abate on the failure of the appellant to bring on record the heirs of the deceased respondent within the time prescribed by law. When legislature clearly intended that the execution proceeding will not abate by artificial reasoning it cannot be said that appeal from such proceeding in execution shall abate to reach a contradictory conclusion to frustrate the execution. When the judgment-debtor prefers an appeal against an order of the executing court obviously passed against him and on the death of the decree holder he intentionally does not substitute the heirs of the decree holder within the time and thereafter allowed the appeal to be dismissed for default then if the appeal abates in spite of the fact that the order of the executing court was not set aside on merit the judgment-debtor will be successful to frustrate the execution of the decree or order. The legislature never intended such result to be reached. Procedural law cannot be interpreted to frustrate the fruits of the decree or order from being enjoyed by the successful party.</u>

7. We therefore find that the learned Subordinate Judge was wholly wrong to hold that the execution case abated due to the death of the respondent during pendency of the said appeal for not substituting his heirs in the High Court Division.

8. It has been well said that real misery of the decree holder starts after the passing of the decree. In this case it really happened. The decree holder filed Money Execution Case No. 55 of 1966 in pursuance of the certificate granted by the then High Court of Dhaka in Matter No. 31 of 1962. Thereafter the judgment-debtor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 208 of 1966 under section 47 of the Code and the same was dismissed on 30.6.67 but the execution case having been dismissed for default on 12.7.67 the decree holder filed Money Execution Case No. 67 of 1968 on 9.12.68 and again the judgment-debtor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1969 under section 47 of the Code and the same was dismissed on 7.6.69. He again filed Miscellaneous Case No. 174 of 1989 under section 47 of the Code and the same was dismissed on 16.1.71. He again filed Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1971 under section 47 of the Code and the same was allowed on 16.1.75 holding that the claim of the decree holder before the High Court in the said Matter No. 31 of 1962 was barred by time and as such the decree could not be executed though the judgment-debtor did not prefer any appeal against the order of the High Court passed against him and allowed the same to stand. This impropriety on the part of the executing Court was noticed by the High Court Division while disposing of the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1975 against the said order of the executing court by observing "the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have travelled well beyond his jurisdiction and competence in questioning the legality of the decree on the ground of limitation. Moreover, the decree in the instant case was passed by the High Court under a special statute and it was not open to the executing court which was a Subordinate Court to question the legality of the decree passed by a Superior Court." In the said judgment the Court below was cautioned with the observation "The subordinate courts would do well to apply their mind a more carefully in such situations before rushing to judgment. We find no reason why the judgment-debtor could not have moved this Court for the redress of his grievance, if any, in accordance with law." In spite of the fact that a copy of the said judgment was before the executing Court again same mistake was committed by the executing court in nullifying the judgment of this court upon written objection filed on 19.1.84 by the opposite parties No. 2 and 3 brought on record as heirs of the deceased judgment-debtor along with opposite party Nos. 3 and 4. We fail to understand how an objection by heirs of the deceased judgment-debtor could be entertained by the Court below after the repeal of section 47 from the Code of Civil Procedure by Ordinance No. 48 of 1983 published in the official Gazette an 5.9.1983. The opposite parties were quite aware of this legal position and hence they did not mention in that objection petition under what provision of the Code they filed the same. The learned Subordinate Judge proceeded to hear the said objection in spite of repeal of section 47 of the Code as if in spite of such repeal he had the inherent power to do so and had the impertinence to set aside the order of this court passed in the said appeal managing to over look the caution expressed by this court in dealing with an order of this court by a subordinate court. We cannot but express our utter frustration and helplessness in such matter. If the subordinate courts go on nullifying orders of the Higher Courts then there will be complete indiscipline in the field of administration of justice and people's confidence in the judiciary will be shaken.

9. The only course open to the opposite parties was to move this Court by way of review of review of the judgment passed in that appeal or by way of an appeal before the Appellate Division to set aside the judgment and order passed by this Court in the said appeal and not by way of filing an objection to the executing court. After the repeal of section 47 of the Code the limited jurisdiction vested in the executing court to decide the questions of execution, discharge and satisfaction of the decree has been taken away to save the decree holder from the misery of facing unlimited number of objections against the execution of the decree and thereby delaying the execution of the decree indefinitely. If the subordinate judiciary goes on frustrating the intention of the legislature by assuming jurisdiction taken away from them by express legislation and the executing court shows the impropriety to nullify judgment and order of this Court in spite of the caution expressed by this Court in the said judgment in appeal from the order dated 16.1.75 passed by the executing court striking out the execution case and restores the said order by the impugned order finding fault with the order of this court motive of the learned Judge in passing the impugned order is obvious.

10. We therefore find that the objection filed by the opposite parties before the executing court was malafide to delay and defeat the execution of the decree passed against their predecessor by this court. The learned Subordinate judge acted illegally in allowing the said objection resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Therefore the impugned order is liable to he set aside and execution case to be proceeded with in accordance with law. The opposite parties are liable to pay compensatory cost to the petitioner for abusing the process of the court for unnecessarily harassing the petitioner.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute with compensatory cost of Tk. 3,000/00 to be paid by the contesting opposite parties No. 2 and 3 to the petitioner within two months. The executing Court is directed to proceed with the execution case in accordance with law.

End.
